reference.title: Quick reference
reference.lede: The cross-cutting material that does not belong to any one topic. This is the page to reopen the night before a test.
reference.summary: Who holds which powers, grants and mandates, key clauses, the two required cases, a timeline, Federalist No. 39

rows: Declare war · coin money · regulate interstate commerce · make treaties · raise an army · naturalize citizens

sections.title: Grants, mandates, and conditions of aid
rows: Money restricted to specific categories of spending
Preferred by the national government · most commonly used
Money for a broad policy area with minimal restrictions
A requirement the national government places on the states
Unfunded mandates are the ones states object to most
A condition attached to nearly all federal grants

sections.title: Constitutional provisions that shape federalism
rows: Basis of implied powers. Read broadly in McCulloch.
National power over interstate commerce. Read broadly from the late 1930s; limited in Lopez.
States honor each other’s public acts, records, and court judgments.
The Constitution and valid federal law prevail over state law. Basis of preemption; applied in McCulloch.
Reserves undelegated powers to the states or the people.
No state may deny due process or equal protection. Basis of selective incorporation.
Federal income tax — the money behind modern grants.
Voters elect senators; state legislatures lose their direct voice in Congress.

sections.title: The two required cases
rows: Congress chartered a national bank. Maryland taxed its Baltimore branch, and the cashier, James McCulloch, refused to pay.
A high school student was convicted under the federal Gun-Free School Zones Act of 1990 for bringing a handgun to school.
Can Congress create a bank? Can a state tax it?
Does the Commerce Clause give Congress power to ban guns in school zones?
Yes, Congress may create the bank (Necessary and Proper Clause). No, Maryland may not tax it (Supremacy Clause). Unanimous.
No. The law exceeded Congress’s commerce power. 5–4.
“Necessary” means appropriate, not indispensable. A state that could tax a federal institution could destroy it.
Gun possession near a school is not economic activity that substantially affects interstate commerce. Upholding the law would give Congress a general police power.

sections.title: Federalist No. 39 — Madison’s five tests
rows: Foundation — how the Constitution is ratified
Federal: ratified by the people acting as separate states
Partly federal, partly national: the House from the people, the Senate from the states
Operation — whom the powers act on
Federal: “certain enumerated objects only”; everything else stays with the states
Neither wholly federal nor wholly national
sections.note: Remember: in Federalist No. 39, “federal” means the states — a league of states, what we would call a confederation. “National” means a government that acts directly on individuals. It is not today’s meaning of “the federal government.”
